messages.author: f4c2e63aec3c6db2
messages.subject: WebAssembly as Stan target?
parts:
On the subject of Stan 3... perhaps there should be a minimal C++ GUI
target (QtStan/GtkStan?) with an eye towards transpiling to JavaScript.
A WebAssembly W3C working group was announced today and it looks like it
will enjoy broad support

- https://blog.mozilla.org/luke/2015/06/17/webassembly/
- https://brendaneich.com/2015/06/from-asm-js-to-webassembly/

Having Stan working in the browser would be great --- and might
potentially solve a lot of the platform headaches.

Best,

Allen

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: WebAssembly as Stan target?
parts:
We've tried (albeit not very hard) with emscripten and PNACL but didn't get very far. Also, Bob nominated Mitzi to thinking about designing a web interface to (basically Cmd) Stan but that hasn't gotten off the ground either. But I do think a web client that ran models locally would be more promising than a mythical high-powered free web server that ran models remotely.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: WebAssembly as Stan target?
parts:
Here's an executive summary of getting to an "install free"
experience for Stan (a very good thing):

1. running models on client side (lightweight server)

PRO: free
CON: can't get it to work

2. running models on server side (heavyweight servers)

2a. interactive (like JuliaBox):
provide RStan, PyStan, Stan.jl or CmdStan

2b. batch (like running on Cluster):
provide "

2c. we build Andrew's simple app

PRO: we know how to do it
CON: have to pay for it somehow

If we pay for it or venture capitalists pay for it, then we
can make it easy for users without installation.

Otherwise, if our users pay, they may have to also do the
equivalent of an install, only remotely. I don't know how easy
we could make it.

I don't think Mitzi's going to have time to do (2c).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: WebAssembly as Stan target?
parts:
On Wednesday, June 17, 2015 at 5:40:59 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Here's an executive summary of getting to an "install free"
experience for Stan (a very good thing):

Or Amazon servers:
  • This guy now installs RStan in his RStudio-On-The-Web AMI http://www.louisaslett.com/RStudio_AMI/
  • We ask him to include ShinyStan, example-models, clang++, etc. next time
  • We can run a "free tier" for the public that can run examples that have been pre-serialized but doesn't have enough RAM to compile an arbitrary model
  • Anyone can clone this AMI, use it on however much hardware they need, and pay Amazon spot rates to do their own research

Or SageMathCloud:

  • We ask them to install various interfaces to Stan
  • Anyone can sign up for a (currently) free account and use Stan via an IPython Notebook

PROS: We don't have to pay for it but we know it is workable

CONS:  Does not have a Stan branded / customized interface


Ben

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Python SageMathCloud;  Amazon EC2 RStudio-on-the-Web
parts:
On Thursday, June 18, 2015 at 3:41:04 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I'll be ecstatic if other people built wrappers for us.  I hadn't
heard about these.  Is an AMI something Andrew could install more
easily than installing RStan?  If so, there's some potential there.
Though I don't know that Andrew could use it on Amtrak, which is
where I hear he gets most of his work done.  :-)

You don't really install an AMI; you just have to have an account to use it. But Amazon's gig is allowing people to rent exactly as much hardware as they need (which might include being able to do some stuff for free as long as you don't have to compile a model) but would mostly be for people whose laptops are not suitable for MCMC.

Is SageMathCloud something that gives poeple free IPython Notebooks?
If so, getting Stan on it would be awesome.  Allen --- could you
help them get Stan implemented?

It (currently) gives people free accounts on the closest thing there is to a high-powered public server that happens to have IPython Notebooks. But an IPython Notebook is not specific to Python (which is why they are changing their name to Jupyter), so you could actually use any interface to Stan that was installed via an IPython Notebook. (IPython notebooks actually render on GitHub now, so it might be good to make one for each of the BUGS examples rather than a knitr document).

Ben

messages.author: f4c2e63aec3c6db2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Python SageMathCloud;  Amazon EC2 RStudio-on-the-Web
parts:
I talked about this with Ben briefly in NYC. If we can find some clever
way to limit usage (maybe some sort of "max n concurrent users"
limitation), I think it wouldn't be hard to have a free public
equivalent of SageMathCloud where RStan and PyStan are both installed. I
only know how to set this thing up using Jupyter/IPython but I suspect
nobody will complain about that (the actual software is this:
https://github.com/jupyter/jupyterhub). I think the user experience
would actually be rather nice at modest cost (maybe $30 a month for a
bunch of concurrent users). The "publicity" would be well worth it.
Nobody would have to install Stan in order to try it out.

(Of course, if we can get the SageMathCloud folks to install RStan or
PyStan we can just direct people there -- and skip this work.)

If I can find the time I'm willing to work on this sort of thing because
it (jupyterhub) is what I used (experimentally) this year when I taught
a Python course.


Best,

Allen
